title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
hook: Krishna in a scholar's book carries a dot under the r, the s and the n, and each dot curls the tongue
carry: let your tongue curl back for it

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, ka, the first consonant, and ka, the first consonant, and the map of the mouth: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips, and c always said ch. We skipped the roof. Today we go there, and look back on the week. Day one thousand forty-three.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.`

segments.voice: Krishna, the way a scholar spells it, has dots hanging under its letters. K. R with a dot. S with a dot. N with a dot. A. Kṛṣṇa. It can look fussy, like footnotes that wandered into the middle of a word. But the dots point to the place we skipped yesterday, the roof of the mouth. They tell the tongue to do one thing: curl back. Today, the dot underneath.
screen: `KṚṢṆA: A DOT UNDER R, S AND N.` → `NOT FOOTNOTES.` → `THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.`

segments.voice: Put the tip of your tongue behind your top teeth and say ta. That's the teeth row. Now slide the tip back along the roof of your mouth, past the ridge, and curl it up a little. Say ta from there. The sound gets deeper, almost hollow. That's the roof row, and in transliteration its letters get a dot underneath: ṭa, ḍa, ṇa. Linguists call these sounds retroflex: made with the tongue bent back. The same curl gives a second kind of sh. Plain sh, written with an accent mark on the s, sits at the palate: Śiva. The s with a dot under it is sh said with the tongue curled back: Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa. And the r with a dot under it is something else again: a vowel. Sanskrit treats a lightly rolled r as a vowel sound in its own right, ṛ. How it's said depends on where you learned it. Some reciters say it close to ri, which is where the English spelling Krishna comes from. Others, in parts of the south and west, say it closer to ru. Both are living ways of saying the same letter. So now the name can be read in full: kṛ, with the r-vowel; ṣ, the curled sh; ṇa, the curled n. And look at the week behind us. The mudras ended with hands that were received, danced, and found everywhere. Then the sounds began: a, the plainest letter; the line that says stay longer; the map of the mouth; and today, the dot that curls the tongue. Hands, then mouth. Each one a way of letting the body carry meaning.
screen: `THE ROOF ROW: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.` · `Ś AT THE PALATE, Ṣ CURLED BACK.` · `Ṛ: THE R THAT IS A VOWEL.` · `THE WEEK: HANDS, THEN MOUTH.` · then, large: `THE DOT MEANS: CURL THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let the jaw hang soft. On an out-breath, say ta at the teeth. Next breath, curl the tongue back and say ṭa at the roof. Go back and forth slowly, a few times, feeling the tongue travel. Then the n: na at the teeth, ṇa at the roof. Then put it together and say the name slowly, piece by piece: kṛ, ṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa. However you've always said it is fine. This is just listening to what the dots ask for. If you pray, you can let the name be said with care. If not, simply notice the tongue at work. The bell holds the time.
Ṛ. The r that is a vowel, alongside the dot underneath that curls the tongue back for ṭ, ḍ, ṇ and ṣ.
Your line: let your tongue curl back for it. Today, when you meet a dot under a letter, let your tongue curl back for it once, even silently. Day one thousand forty-three.

howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit practice the retroflex row (ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa) by curling the tongue back to the roof of the mouth, and recite names like Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu with these sounds.

fork.setup: you're reading Kṛṣṇa aloud and reach the ṛ. how do reciters say it?
options: close to ri, or close to ru, depending on where they learned.
fork.reveal: ṛ is a vowel. some reciters say it close to ri, the source of the spelling Krishna; others, in parts of the south and west, say it closer to ru.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: ṛ, the r that is a vowel, as in Kṛṣṇa.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dots under Kṛṣṇa are a scholar's fuss.
what it means: each dot tells the tongue to curl back, and ṛ is an r used as a vowel.
what a scholar hears: the retroflex series ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇ, with ṣ; ṛ is syllabic, said ri by some reciters and ru by others, in parts of the south and west.
